results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book shows you how to build a chroma keyer from scratch, then honestly advises you not to bother. The recipe mirrors the homemade luma keyer from earlier in the chapter: start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV, then pipe the HSV image into a color curve. In that curve, the red channel now contains Hue data, green contains Saturation, and blue contains Value (brightness), so you adjust the three curves to include or exclude the hue, saturation, and value ranges of the target object [S1].

The core definition behind it: a chroma keyer converts RGB to an HSV/HSL representation internally because saturation isn't an RGB attribute, sets a starting pixel as the "center" of the key, then defines separate ranges for hue, saturation, and value — pixels inside go to white, outside go to black [S13]. That makes it more discriminating than a color-blind luma key, since it considers both chrominance and luminance [S14].

The book's verdict on the DIY version is candid: unlike the luma key, where being clever can yield real improvements over the basic keyer, a homemade chroma keyer will "probably be more hassle than it's worth" — try it once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf keyer is "hard to improve upon" [S2]. It does offer one more flexible variation: a homemade **3D chroma keyer** that works on utterly different principles, keying on any arbitrary color via a grossly simplified version of Primatte's operating approach [S7]. A test image called "Chroma key target.tif" is provided for practicing both chroma and luma keys [S5].

Practical considerations the book raises:

- **Soft edges require tolerances:** a raw range-based key is very hard-edged, so any worthwhile chroma keyer needs tolerance settings for hue, saturation, and value [S13].
- **Terminology:** a chroma keyer specifically keys on chrominance and luminance after an RGB→HSV/HSL conversion; most greenscreen tools (Keylight, Ultimatte, the Delta keyer) are actually color difference keyers, while Primatte is a sophisticated 3D chroma keyer — though the book uses "keyer" for all of them [S4][S6][S8].
- **Workflow advice:** try a chroma key first because it's quick; if it doesn't produce nice edges, switch to a color difference key, which usually gives much cleaner results [S15].

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
The book treats nonsquare pixels as a property of a format, not of the monitor: they are pixels whose width and height are not equal, so the pixel's shape is rectangular rather than square [S2][S3][S4]. The ratio of width to height is the **pixel aspect ratio** (PAR), measured separately from the image's own aspect ratio [S3][S10]. A normally adjusted computer monitor has square pixels with a PAR of 1:1 [S1].

## Definition and pixel aspect ratio

The book stresses not confusing PAR with the image aspect ratio — they are usually different numbers [S11]. For example, NTSC analog video uses a PAR of 10:11, meaning pixels are slightly taller than they are wide; a perfectly round circle created on a computer would appear as an ellipse, stretched 11/10ths vertically, when sent to an SD video monitor. You may need to scale the image manually (or rely on software that automates it) to compensate [S11]. Similarly, standard-definition video uses rectangular pixels overall — 720×480 (NTSC) and 720×576 (PAL) — while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors use square pixels [S8].

## Why and how they're used in cinema

The book explains that some film and video formats display an image with a different aspect ratio than the original digital image, and those systems are said to have nonsquare pixels [S2]. In cinema this usually happens with **anamorphic (squeezed) formats** — images that are optically distorted and restored to their correct shape when projected. The most common is Cinemascope, whose 2:1 squeeze is used as the book's example because it's the most dramatic [S6][S7]. Importantly, "displaying nonsquare pixels" doesn't mean the pixels on your monitor actually look stretched: the system performs a temporary unsqueeze, a geometric transformation for display only, and the underlying image data is never modified [S5].

The reason behind all this is implicit in the book's framing: the stored image carries a distorted aspect ratio that is corrected at display time, letting a wide image be held in a standard frame. The cited passages don't spell out the efficiency argument (e.g., film-stock or bandwidth savings) explicitly — that part is a natural inference from the 2:1 squeeze rather than something the book states.

## Compositing pitfalls

Working with squeezed formats requires care, especially with rotations: rotating an element while it's still squeezed, then unsqueezing, produces distortion. The correct order is to unsqueeze, rotate, and re-squeeze along the x-axis [S9]. Even a small 5-degree rotation shows visible problems on a round subject, so the book's advice is to double-check everything when working with nonsquare pixels [S9].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
Francis Glebas's "Miscellaneous Drawing Tips" in *Directing the Story* is a checklist for storytelling-driven drawing: clarity, boldness, and physical empathy come before polish [S3][S6]. The tips fall into three groups.

## Clarity and intent

- Draw for clarity — one idea per sketch — and draw attention to one idea at a time, just as you would when speaking [S3][S7].
- Highlight the sketch's key idea and subordinate everything else to it [S6].
- Don't get too clever: tricky camera angles often just make the drawing ambiguous [S6].
- Have something to say in your image; don't doodle [S3].
- If part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and rework it — don't be afraid to redraw and search for the best solution [S3].

## Boldness and readable design

- Draw bold — grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil, never a hard pencil — and number your drawings; they should read from across the room [S2].
- A drawing should survive being blackened in and still read clearly; keep decoration inside the main outline, and make the outlines interesting [S1].
- Avoid symmetry, which is boring and makes drawings look cut out; use angles for dynamic asymmetry [S6].
- Play straight lines against curves for interest [S3].
- Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S6].

## Feeling the pose

- Show how the character feels: feel the pose and the emotion in your own body as you draw [S6].
- A person is always "doing" something — express the purpose and experience the pose kinetically [S6].
- Darken pupils when drawing eyes [S3].
- Use straight line symbols for stretches, bent line symbols for squashes [S6].
- Watch the body's landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S6].

The through-line is that drawing serves the story: one clear idea, a bold readable image, and a body you inhabit while drawing. Glebas treats the artist's own physical experience as the instrument for making the image feel alive [S6].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The VES Handbook frames the choice as a question of how different the two displays are: the complexity of transforming image data optimized for one display into data optimized for another depends directly on the degree of difference between them [S2]. **Transcoding** is for displays that differ only modestly; **color rerendering** is the best solution when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S1][S2].

| Aspect | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| When to use | Displays match in black level, white luminance, gamma, and viewing conditions, but differ in primary chromaticities [S2] | Displays differ grossly in contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions [S1] |
| What it does | Re-encodes the same colors for the new display | Undoes the first display's color rendering, then renders the image anew for the second display [S1] |
| Workflow | Linearize display 1's encoded RGB → convert to CIE XYZ → convert to RGB for display 2 → reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S2] | Undo any color rendering (implicit or explicit) done for display 1, then color render the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values for display 2 [S1] |
| Complexity | Lower — a straight mathematical re-encoding [S2] | Higher — required only when the intended appearance itself must change |

For transcoding, the pipeline is a pure color-space conversion:

```text
display 1 encoded RGB → linearize → CIE XYZ → display 2 RGB → reimpose encoding nonlinearity
```

Color rendering in the handbook's language means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — for example, a still camera's JPEG encodes a desert scene so it looks right on an office monitor whose peak white is hundreds of times dimmer than desert sunlight [S4]. Rerendering therefore has to first strip out that baked-in adjustment before applying a new one for the destination display [S1]. This is why raw camera encodings are easier to rerender: no color rendering has been baked in, so it can be done downstream [S6]. The practical takeaway: nearly identical displays call for transcoding; large environmental differences call for color rerendering [S2].

results.question: What does the book say about FACE OFF?
results.answer:
The only "face-off" the corpus defines is a **stunt-fall technique** in *The Screen Combat Handbook*, not a reference to a film. A face-off is a fall that starts face-first, but the performer tucks and rotates at the last moment to land on their back instead [S1].

So the keyword does double duty in context: in the glossary it names a controlled combat-fall move, while elsewhere the corpus uses "face off" loosely to describe two fighters squaring up in fighting stances [S5]. If you meant the 1997 John Woo film *Face/Off*, that title doesn't appear anywhere in the retrieved material — the closest technical concept in the evidence is **face paste**, the VFX practice of capturing facial motion separately and compositing it onto body animation [S11].

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The corpus's "book" is the movement-control handbook, and section 6.1 is literally titled "Affect, fatigue, and injury are control states." Its core thesis: these are not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen — each one must actually **change later action selection and execution** [S4]. The same rule appears in the fight-specimen invariants, where the injury must persist through every frame and no action boundary may discard it [S5].

| State | How the handbook specifies it | What it must change |
|---|---|---|
| **Affect** | An appraisal update on valence–arousal–dominance: trigger → appraisal scores (goal congruence, controllability, certainty) → prior/posterior VAD → behavioral effects [S4] | Attention focus, recovery urgency, risk tolerance [S4] |
| **Fatigue** | A compiler-style accumulator: `f = clamp(f + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1)`, tracked globally (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) and per-limb as local capacity [S2][S3] | Step-width variability, stabilization time, trunk contribution [S2] |
| **Injury** | An object with region, pain 0–10, severity, capacity multipliers (load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off) and compensations, with confidence marked as dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement [S8] | Loading strategy, stance intervals, trunk lean during recovery [S8] |

Two design points matter. First, fatigue is explicitly **fatigue, not remaining capacity** — it accumulates work and impact and decays by recovery, and the work/impact/recovery terms must be calibrated because they cannot be inferred from prose [S3]. Second, affect is deliberately underdetermined: dimensional affect gives a continuous trajectory, but the same high-arousal negative state can read as fear, anger, pain, or disgust depending on appraisal and context [S6]. That is why the specimen wires a concrete instance — an appraisal of goal congruence −0.72 with controllability 0.34 — into behavioral outcomes like narrowed attention and one risky recovery attempt [S4].

On the **"in cinema" framing, the evidence has a gap**: the handbook treats these three states as character-control architecture for filmed fight sequences (audio binds, camera and editorial assembly are downstream of state commits) [S5][S13], but the retrieved corpus contains no film-theory or editing analysis of affect, fatigue, and injury as control states — the Dancyger pages in evidence are only filmographies [S11][S14][S15]. The adjacent movement literature covers a different "state" concept, the six Laban Effort states (mobile, stable, remote, rhythm, dream, awake) built from two-factor combinations of Effort [S1][S7], with experiential exercises and the four weight–flow combinations in each state detailed in the Laban workbook [S12]; pain's effect on breath, voice pitch, and the adrenaline masking of injury is covered in stage-combat literature [S9]. If you need a source that analyzes affect/fatigue/injury as control states specifically in cinema, that account is absent from the corpus, and the closest available claim is the handbook's production-pipeline one.

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The sources in your corpus converge on a single idea: on screen, an object's movement is only perceptible in relation to what surrounds it — the frame line and, above all, the background. Bruce Block puts it directly: visual movement can be produced only when an object moves in relation to the frame line; when nothing changes position against the frame, the image is static [S8]. The background is the stationary yardstick against which that movement is seen and measured — **relative movement** is literally "movement gauged by its changing position relative to a second, stationary object" [S3]. Block's forest example makes the mechanism vivid: when a camera pans to follow a car that stays centered in the frame, the trees in the background slide the opposite way, and the viewer transfers that apparent movement to the car — which is technically not moving relative to the frame at all [S13].

The same perceptual transfer, in reverse, is **induced movement**: a moving object can hand its motion off to a nearby stationary one, so the stationary object appears to move while the moving one seems still [S1]. Together these explain why backgrounds are never passive — they are the reference system that turns a body's travel into visible motion.

## Techniques that play the background against the object

- **Motion parallax** — moving players or the camera so subjects cross in front of, or are partially covered by, foreground objects produces different image-travel speeds at different distances, which conveys each object's position and distance to the viewer [S10].
- **Tracking alongside** — the simplest motivated move: tracking parallel to a character or vehicle emphasizes the moving background and the sweep of motion behind the subject [S12].
- **Telephoto circular tracking** — circling a static subject with a long lens makes the background seem to revolve rapidly behind them; the effect accelerates with greater subject-to-background distance, faster camera movement, and longer focal length [S9].
- **Compositing/match moving** — when the foreground camera moves, the background must move accordingly; tracking data is extracted from the foreground footage and applied to the background, a process called match moving [S6]. In practice this is done with tracker tools (e.g., in DaVinci Resolve) that attach background elements to the foreground camera's motion [S4].

## Purpose and effect

The background exists functionally, not just decoratively, in this scheme. Parallax and relative movement give the audience spatial information — where things sit in depth and how fast they travel [S10] — and every moving object generates a **track**, its path through the frame, which can be described by direction, quality, scale, and speed and used to create continuity of movement across cuts [S5][S7][S14]. Beyond information, manipulating the object–background relationship is an expressive tool: the spinning-background telephoto shot is specifically used to visualize a character's psychological breakdown or intense inner turmoil, the world seeming to spin out of control around them [S9]. So movement with a background is both how film measures motion and how it manufactures meaning from it.

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
The sources describe sound editing as the post-production craft of building and mixing a film's complete soundtrack — dialogue, effects, music, ambient atmosphere, and voice-overs — whose two primary goals are narrative clarity and believability [S1][S6][S8]. Everything the production did not capture in original sound is created or re-created during the sound edit [S1].

## What it aims at

The most urgent task of the sound edit is to create **believable sound**, because sound is processed by viewers more rapidly than visuals: if the sound doesn't seem believable, the visuals are undermined and audience involvement is lost [S8]. The editor's first task is determining the narrative point of the scene and surrounding it with sound, as in *The Battle of Algiers*, where authenticity of sound is central to the story's involvement [S1]. During the rough sound edit the goal parallels the picture edit — believability of performance and a progressive sense of story — while dramatic emphasis and metaphor are deferred to the fine cut; the editor also decides how much or how little dialogue is needed [S9].

## How it's done

During the rough cut, only the tracks needed for dramatic decisions are used (dialogue and occasional scratch music). After picture lock, the editor and sound designer build the multi-track design **one track at a time**, then equalize and mix down to a master — stereo at the simplest, 5.1 surround for cinema [S6]. Track counts vary widely: roughly 6–16 for simple films [S6], up to 60 tracks in a feature film [S13], and 62 or more in a blockbuster [S4]. Sound editors think in two dimensions at once: horizontally along time (one sound following another) and vertically as simultaneous layers — freeway noise, birds, a plane overhead, footsteps — integrated like a musician's tapestry [S10].

Common techniques include separating sound effects to allow smooth fades from one sound to the next, and using a continuing sound across two disparate visuals to imply a link between scenes, whether connecting or separating time and space [S13]. Editors also experiment with speed, pitch, timbre, and direction of effects [S11], and acquire additional audio files in post to augment or replace production sound and generate a more realistic "reality" [S7].

## Why it matters

Sound editing is considered more elaborate than picture editing — it demands more decisions, and a wrong one can readily undermine the visuals [S1]. Without an effective soundtrack, the visuals will not succeed [S1], and creative sound affects audiences on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels [S5]. "Silent" films were never intended to be silent; music always accompanied screenings, and sound editing continues to earn major awards [S4][S5]. Historically, early sync sound actually inhibited editing — dialog scenes couldn't be cut without losing synchronization, and a cut meant losing both sound and image, restricting editors to silent sequences until rerecording and multiple-camera techniques arrived [S14].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The book's core advice is to write radio scripts with far fewer words than you think you need — lean, bare-bones copy. The metaphor it uses: if a 60-second spot is a house, a 30-second spot is a tent [S1]. And since most radio spots are promotional, clients often want promo tags tacked onto the end, which cuts into your total time — so you have to write sparely to make room [S1].

Why spare writing works: it lets the voice talent read slowly — quietly, one word at a time — and the book argues there's "remarkable power in silence," which is to radio what white space is to print: silence enlarges the idea it surrounds [S2][S7]. Bare-bones execution is what actually leaps out of the radio [S7]. The one exception is if your concept genuinely demands lots of words and fast action [S2].

The practical warning is just as strong: even if your idea isn't a bare-bones kind of idea, write sparely anyway. There's nothing worse than showing up at the studio with a fat script, because you'll be forced to edit under pressure and without client approval [S3]. The Adweek handbook adds a complementary point — radio works through repetition — so the message itself should stay simple, clean, and easy to comprehend [S8][S15].
